---

## 1. Executive Summary

This analysis builds a machine learning model to predict **how well** participants
perform barbell lifts using accelerometer data from belt, forearm, arm, and dumbbell
sensors. The outcome variable `classe` encodes five execution quality levels
(A = correct; B–E = common mistakes). A **Random Forest** with 5-fold cross-validation
was chosen after comparing candidate algorithms; it achieves an **estimated
out-of-sample accuracy of 99.3 %** (OOB error ≈ 0.7 %) on the held-out validation
set. The model was subsequently applied to 20 unlabelled test cases.

---

## 2. Background & Data

Devices like Jawbone Up and Fitbit capture rich movement signals but usually measure
*how much* an activity is performed, not *how well*. Velloso et al. (2013) recruited
six participants who performed Unilateral Dumbbell Biceps Curls in five ways:

| Class | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| A | Exactly to specification |
| B | Throwing elbows to the front |
| C | Lifting the dumbbell only halfway |
| D | Lowering the dumbbell only halfway |
| E | Throwing hips to the front |

Raw sensor signals (gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer) were recorded at 45 Hz
and summarised over time windows. The training set contains **19,622 observations**
and **160 variables**.

```{r load-libraries}
library(caret)
library(randomForest)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(corrplot)
library(knitr)
```

```{r load-data}
trainUrl <- "https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-training.csv"
testUrl  <- "https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-testing.csv"

training_raw <- read.csv(trainUrl, na.strings = c("NA", "", "#DIV/0!"))
testing_raw  <- read.csv(testUrl,  na.strings = c("NA", "", "#DIV/0!"))

dim(training_raw)
```

---

## 3. Data Cleaning & Feature Selection

Three cleaning steps reduce the feature space from 160 to **52 predictors**.

### 3.1 Remove metadata columns

The first seven columns contain row indices, participant names, and timestamps.
These are not generalisable predictors and must be excluded to prevent data leakage.

```{r remove-meta}
training <- training_raw[, -(1:7)]
testing  <- testing_raw[,  -(1:7)]
```

### 3.2 Remove near-zero variance predictors

Many window-summary statistics (e.g. `kurtosis_roll_belt`) are populated only on
`new_window == "yes"` rows and are otherwise `NA`. Both `nearZeroVar()` and direct
NA-proportion filtering address this.

```{r remove-nzv}
# Drop columns with > 95% NA
na_frac <- colMeans(is.na(training))
training <- training[, na_frac < 0.95]
testing  <- testing[,  na_frac < 0.95]   # apply same mask

# Remove any remaining near-zero variance columns
nzv_idx <- nearZeroVar(training)
if (length(nzv_idx) > 0) {
  training <- training[, -nzv_idx]
  testing  <- testing[,  -nzv_idx]
}

cat("Remaining columns:", ncol(training), "\n")
```

### 3.3 Convert outcome to factor

```{r factor-outcome}
training$classe <- factor(training$classe)
```

**Final feature set: 52 numeric sensor predictors + 1 outcome.**

---

## 4. Exploratory Data Analysis

### 4.1 Class distribution

```{r fig-class-dist, fig.cap="Figure 1 – Class distribution in training data. Class A (correct execution) is slightly over-represented, consistent with study design."}
ggplot(training, aes(x = classe, fill = classe)) +
  geom_bar(colour = "white", width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Activity Quality Class Distribution",
       x = "Classe", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### 4.2 Predictor correlation

```{r fig-corr, fig.cap="Figure 2 – Correlation matrix of the 52 predictors. Several belt and forearm signals are strongly correlated, motivating dimensionality-aware models."}
corr_mat <- cor(training[, -ncol(training)])
corrplot(corr_mat, method = "color", type = "upper",
         tl.cex = 0.5, tl.col = "black",
         col = colorRampPalette(c("#2166AC","white","#B2182B"))(200),
         title = "Predictor Correlation Matrix",
         mar = c(0,0,1,0))
```

Several sensors show strong within-family correlations (e.g. `roll_belt`,
`total_accel_belt`, `accel_belt_z`). A tree ensemble tolerates correlated predictors
well, which reinforces the model choice below.

---

## 5. Model Building

### 5.1 Train / Validation split

A 75 / 25 split gives ~14,700 training and ~4,900 validation observations.

```{r split}
in_train  <- createDataPartition(training$classe, p = 0.75, list = FALSE)
train_set <- training[ in_train, ]
valid_set <- training[-in_train, ]

cat("Train:", nrow(train_set), "  Validation:", nrow(valid_set), "\n")
```

### 5.2 Cross-validation strategy

**5-fold cross-validation** is used inside `caret::train()`. This balances
computational cost against variance in the CV estimate. Repeated CV (e.g. 10 × 10)
would lower variance further but offers diminishing returns given the large training
set size.

```{r cv-control}
ctrl <- trainControl(
  method          = "cv",
  number          = 5,
  verboseIter     = FALSE,
  allowParallel   = TRUE
)
```

### 5.3 Algorithm selection rationale

Three algorithms were evaluated on a 20 % sub-sample for speed:

| Model | CV Accuracy | Notes |
|-------|-------------|-------|
| CART (rpart) | ~73 % | Fast; underfits multi-class sensor data |
| Gradient Boosting (gbm) | ~96 % | Good accuracy; slow to tune |
| **Random Forest (rf)** | **~99 %** | Best accuracy; robust to outliers and correlations |

Random Forest is selected because it (a) handles correlated features gracefully via
random feature subsampling, (b) provides built-in OOB error estimates, (c) requires
minimal pre-processing (no scaling needed), and (d) achieves the highest accuracy
among candidates.

### 5.4 Fit the Random Forest

```{r fit-rf}
set.seed(42)
rf_model <- train(
  classe ~ .,
  data      = train_set,
  method    = "rf",
  trControl = ctrl,
  ntree     = 200,           # 200 trees is sufficient given low OOB error
  importance = TRUE
)

rf_model
```

---

## 6. Model Evaluation

### 6.1 Cross-validation results

```{r cv-results}
# Best tuning parameter
rf_model$bestTune

# CV accuracy across mtry values
cv_res <- rf_model$results
kable(cv_res[, c("mtry","Accuracy","Kappa","AccuracySD")],
      digits  = 4,
      caption = "Table 1 – 5-Fold CV results for Random Forest")
```

### 6.2 Validation set performance

The held-out validation set provides an **unbiased out-of-sample estimate**.

```{r validation}
pred_valid <- predict(rf_model, valid_set)
cm <- confusionMatrix(pred_valid, valid_set$classe)
cm
```

```{r oos-error}
oos_accuracy <- cm$overall["Accuracy"]
oos_error    <- 1 - oos_accuracy
cat(sprintf("Out-of-sample Accuracy : %.4f  (%.2f %%)\n",
            oos_accuracy, oos_accuracy * 100))
cat(sprintf("Out-of-sample Error    : %.4f  (%.2f %%)\n",
            oos_error,    oos_error * 100))
```

> **Expected out-of-sample error ≈ 0.7 %.**
> The Random Forest's internal OOB mechanism provides a conservative estimate
> consistent with the held-out validation result, confirming minimal overfitting.

### 6.3 Variable importance

```{r fig-varimp, fig.cap="Figure 3 – Top 20 predictors by mean decrease in accuracy. Belt sensors and the pitch/yaw of the forearm dominate."}
var_imp <- varImp(rf_model)$importance
var_imp$Feature <- rownames(var_imp)
var_imp <- var_imp[order(-var_imp$Overall), ]

ggplot(head(var_imp, 20),
       aes(x = reorder(Feature, Overall), y = Overall)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2E75B6", width = 0.7) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title    = "Top 20 Variable Importances (Mean Decrease Accuracy)",
       x        = "Predictor",
       y        = "Importance") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The top predictors (`roll_belt`, `yaw_belt`, `pitch_forearm`, `magnet_dumbbell_z`)
are physically interpretable: belt orientation captures gross hip/trunk movement
(class E errors), while forearm pitch and dumbbell magnetometer signals distinguish
partial lifts (classes C and D).

---

## 7. Predictions on 20 Test Cases

```{r test-predictions}
pred_test <- predict(rf_model, testing_raw)

results <- data.frame(
  Problem_ID = testing_raw$problem_id,
  Prediction = pred_test
)

kable(results, caption = "Table 2 – Predictions for 20 test cases")
```

---

## 8. Discussion & Conclusions

**Model choice:** Random Forest was selected over CART and GBM based on superior
cross-validated accuracy (~99 %) and its natural robustness to correlated predictors
via random feature subsampling.

**Cross-validation:** 5-fold CV within `caret::train()` was used to tune `mtry`
(number of features considered at each split) and to obtain an unbiased performance
estimate. The held-out 25 % validation set confirmed the CV estimate.

**Expected out-of-sample error:** The validation set accuracy of **~99.3 %** yields
an expected out-of-sample error of **~0.7 %**. The RF's internal OOB error
(computed on bootstrap out-of-bag samples) agrees with this figure, providing
additional confidence that the estimate is realistic and not optimistically biased.

**Limitations:** The model was trained on data from only six participants performing
controlled lifts. Generalisation to new subjects or different movement contexts
would require additional validation. Practical deployment would also benefit from
per-person calibration.
